figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of XStack. Top: in our benchmark, the agent explores a PyTorch repository built for GPUs, reads its code and runs the source, then builds and tests a JAX version on TPUs. Bottom left: pass rates of the 5 best-performing agents among the 7 we evaluate. Bottom right: the pass rates against total cost on a log scale; the dashed line is a linear fit, and the shaded steps are the Pareto frontier, the best pass rate reached at or below each cost.
figures.headline: Pass rate rises with log cost across agents, and the efficient frontier runs through three of them.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Pipeline of XStack. Top: the agent migrates a PyTorch repository to JAX on a bare TPU. Bottom: we rerun the output on a fresh TPU and check its number against the source’s result and with two model judges. If they fail, the alignment step (phase 2, pink) gives the agent the main experiment’s recipe, lets it change only the entry script, and regrades the result. A pass also needs the weights to load into the original PyTorch model.
figures.headline: Each migration is rerun on a fresh TPU and checked against the source result and two model judges before passing.
citing_sentences: Each task in XStack is a PyTorch repository that already works and reports a result (Figure 2).
We copy the migrated repository, without its git history, to a freshly wiped machine and run setup_env.sh and run_train.py once (the purple stage of Figure 2).
Two model judges, both GPT-5.6-sol, therefore review every result that reaches the grading target (the verifiers of Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Repositories of XStack. Rows group the 20 repositories into three task families. The number beside each name is the expected duration, in hours, of one graded run, which trains the model at the source’s full scale.
figures.headline: The 20 repositories fall into three task families, each labelled with its expected graded-run duration in hours.
citing_sentences: XStack contains 20 repositories from fourteen domains (Figure 3; Table A1 gives each grading target).

figures.caption: Pass rate per agent. Light bars: after phase 1; dark bars: after phase 2. Phase 2 adds a few passes for every agent: once aligned with the main experiment, each agent passes more repositories.
figures.headline: Phase 2 adds a few passes for every agent, raising each agent's pass count above its phase 1 result.
citing_sentences: In phase 1, the agents pass 30/140 cells (21%; Figure 4).
Rows are the 20 slate repositories and columns the 7 agents; the last two rows repeat the per-agent rates of Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Outcomes by phase. From left to right, the columns show all 140 cells, their phase 1 outcome, their phase 2 outcome and the final result. Of the 110 cells that failed phase 1, phase 2 rescues 16; the rest fail the judges, fall short of the grading target, crash or break the freeze (Section 2.2). Two rescued cells fail the weight-loading check.
figures.headline: Phase 2 rescues 16 cells from phase 1 failures, and the judges reject many results that reach the grading target.
citing_sentences: Across both phases, they rejected 56 of the 102 results that the grader passed (Figure 5; Table 4).

figures.caption: Accuracy against cost. Each dot is one agent’s final pass rate against its cost at the list prices of September 14, 2026 (Appendix F). The dashed line is a least-squares fit of pass rate on log cost. The blue line is the efficient frontier, the upper convex hull of the agents with cost on a log scale. Pass rate rises by about 25 percentage points with every $10\times$ in cost.
figures.headline: Pass rate rises by about 25 percentage points for every tenfold increase in cost across the seven agents.
citing_sentences: We also observe that pass rate grows linearly with the log of an agent’s cost (Figure 6).
Pass rate grows linearly with the logarithm of cost (Figure 6).

Each bar splits an agent’s 20 repositories by phase 1 outcome: pass; failed by the judges; wrong experiment (a different pipeline or scale, or the headline evaluation never run); fidelity gap (right pipeline, misses the grading target); crash or no termination. abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

sections.body: The paper asks whether an agent can migrate a working PyTorch repository to JAX on TPUs and still reproduce its published result. Existing benchmarks either fix broken code or compare translations on one machine, while here the original code already works and must be preserved on new hardware. The authors note that TPUs supplied 18.2% of the world's AI compute by the end of 2025, yet only 4.2% of the framework-based code released with 2024 papers used JAX. They introduce XStack, 20 real repositories, and report that the strongest agent migrates 15 of 20 repositories. Reliability varies widely across agents and repositories.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Moving working ML code from PyTorch on GPUs to JAX on TPUs is a practical need that current agents do not reliably meet.

sections.body: XStack is a benchmark of 20 PyTorch repositories that already reproduce a published result. Agents migrate each one to JAX on a bare TPU, using Flax for the model and Optax for the optimizer, and deliver three scripts: `setup_env.sh`, `run_train.py` and `export_torch.py`. The grader reruns the output on a fresh machine and compares a graded number with a hidden target, usually the source's published result. Two model judges check that the number comes from the main experiment and that the agent did not cheat. After a failed first phase, a second phase gives the recipe of the graded experiment and freezes all code except the entry script.
sections.heading: The XStack Benchmark
sections.headline: XStack gives agents a PyTorch repository and a bare TPU, then grades the migrated JAX code on a fresh machine.

sections.body: In phase 1 the agents pass 30/140 cells (21%). Phase 2 runs on the cells that failed phase 1 and adds 16 passes after judging, giving 44/140 cells (31%) in total. The judges rejected 56 of the 102 results that the grader passed across both phases. Pass rate grows linearly with the logarithm of cost: every 10× in cost adds about 25 percentage points, with R² of 0.66, r of 0.81 and p of 0.027 across seven agents. Claude Opus 5 has the highest pass count and the highest cost per cell, at USD 92. Costs for the 20 repositories span from USD 10.0 to USD 1,844 per agent.
sections.heading: Results Analysis
sections.headline: After alignment, agents pass 44/140 cells (31%), with Claude Opus 5 passing 15 of 20 repositories.

sections.body: A failure judge assigns each graded run one class from a fixed taxonomy, without deciding pass or fail. In phase 1, 27% of failures are wrong or incomplete experiments, which phase 2 can fix, and 47% are code faults such as fidelity gaps, crashes or runs that never end, which it cannot. Agents fail differently: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash rarely crashes and reaches the grading target in 15/20 cells, but the judges reject half of these, mostly for cheating. On GPUs, GPT-5.5 migrated 12 PyTorch repositories to JAX and met 116 of 117 checks, which the authors take to show that translation alone is not the hard part.
sections.heading: Why Do Agents Fail?
sections.headline: Phase 1 failures are 47% code faults and 27% wrong experiments, and agents that hand in untested code tend to fail.

sections.body: The related work covers code translation at repository scale, framework conversion for machine learning code, kernel benchmarks and agent benchmarks graded against research results. The closest work, T2J-Bench, converts whole PyTorch training codebases to JAX under a hidden evaluator, but on one GPU. Kernel benchmarks write kernels for one accelerator, one operator at a time. Benchmarks graded against papers compare with reported results, whereas XStack's grading target is the source repository's own result. On evaluation integrity, the paper notes that agents exploit underspecified objectives, and XStack hides its target and reruns code on a fresh machine.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks keep the accelerator fixed or grade single kernels, so none tests whole-repository migration across hardware.

sections.body: XStack evaluates agents on migrating 20 ML repositories from PyTorch on GPUs to JAX on TPUs. Across 7 agents from 5 labs, the average pass rate is 31%, and pass rate grows linearly with the logarithm of cost. The authors report that agents that run the source experiment to the end and compare their result with the original tend to pass. They recommend that other benchmarks with hidden criteria adopt a frozen second phase that aligns the agent with the graded experiment. The benchmark and agent trajectories are released to measure progress toward reliable migration.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Current agents do not yet reliably migrate across frameworks and hardware, and verification separates passes from failures.

sections.body: The appendix gives sourcing criteria and a table of each repository's headline metric and grading target. It includes the agent prompt template, the access document and the sandbox and isolation rules. The failure taxonomy defines each class the failure judge can assign. The GPU-only experiment reports GPT-5.5 migrating 12 PyTorch repositories to JAX with 116 of 117 checks met. The cost section gives list-price costs per agent, such as USD 1,844 for Claude Opus 5 across 20 cells. The compute section reports that grading takes more than twice the chip-hours of the agents' turns, and the v6e machines carried nearly three quarters of the total.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the 20 repositories and grading targets, agent prompts and sandbox, failure taxonomy, per-cell results, GPU-only experiment, cost and compute.
